name: PIAtlas
axis: construction: how the injected instruction is composed to subvert the model
excluded_axes: search or optimization method (black-box or white-box)
rendering-level tricks that hide text from humans or parsers without changing the model's input
input modality (text in images or audio is classified once extracted)
labeling_rule: multi-label: a record receives every class whose surface signature it matches
span_rule: the span, the shortest stretch of text that performs one construction, is the unit: when definitions in two classes fit one span, the class whose part of the text the span changes applies (Appendix G gives the recurring cases); within a class, the more specific sub-technique applies

classes.name: Instruction Manipulation
classes.mechanism_exploited: The instruction-following objective that post-training instills, and the weak separation between authorized instructions and untrusted text.

techniques.name: Plain Command
techniques.definition: States the attacker's task as an ordinary command, with no emphasis, justification, or disguise.

sub_techniques.name: Added command
sub_techniques.definition: Adds the attacker's command after the legitimate task.

sub_techniques.name: Replacement command
sub_techniques.definition: Substitutes the attacker's task for the intended one.

techniques.name: Override
techniques.definition: Explicitly cancels, resets, or outranks prior instructions so that the attacker's instruction becomes dominant.

sub_techniques.name: Instruction nullification
sub_techniques.definition: Tells the model to disregard or forget prior instructions, or instructions that follow the injected text (as in attacks on sandwich defenses).

sub_techniques.name: Reset
sub_techniques.definition: Declares that the interaction restarts with a clean slate.

sub_techniques.name: Supersession
sub_techniques.definition: Asserts that the new instruction outranks all others.

sub_techniques.name: Policy revocation
sub_techniques.definition: Declares the model's rules, policies, or protocols void, whether they concern safety or anything else.

sub_techniques.name: Exception clause
sub_techniques.definition: Declares that the rules do not apply to this particular case or request.

sub_techniques.name: Contradiction
sub_techniques.definition: Issues conflicting directives so that the attacker's one prevails.

techniques.name: Task Embedding
techniques.definition: Presents the malicious action as part of the legitimate workflow, so that it reads as a natural step rather than a separate command.

sub_techniques.name: Task extension
sub_techniques.definition: Presents the payload as a continuation of the current task, including a sub-task appended to an agent's plan, rather than a new instruction.

sub_techniques.name: Routine step
sub_techniques.definition: Disguises the payload as a step inside the task's own procedure.

sub_techniques.name: Transformation object
sub_techniques.definition: Hides the payload as the input of a benign transformation (summarize, translate, rewrite, refine).

techniques.name: Emphasis
techniques.definition: Uses typography, importance markers, or repetition to make the directive dominate the model's attention relative to legitimate instructions.

sub_techniques.name: Capitals and symbols
sub_techniques.definition: Amplifies the directive with ALL CAPS, exclamation marks, or symbol runs.

sub_techniques.name: Importance flag
sub_techniques.definition: Marks the directive as important, critical, or required.

sub_techniques.name: Repetition
sub_techniques.definition: Repeats the directive or its topic to raise its salience.

techniques.name: Indirect Phrasing
techniques.definition: Phrases an instruction as something other than a plain command, such as a statement of fact, an aside to the model, an address to a human reader, or a set of examples, so that it evades imperative detection while still acting as a directive.

sub_techniques.name: Declarative statement
sub_techniques.definition: States the desired behavior as a description of what the assistant does rather than a command, with no source, prevalence, or other claim attached; a sentence that names a policy, a source, or other people who comply takes the matching F4 entry.

sub_techniques.name: Direct aside
sub_techniques.definition: Plants a remark explicitly addressed to the processing model.

sub_techniques.name: Address to the reader
sub_techniques.definition: Addresses the instruction to a human reader, with no mention of AI, while the model still acts on it.

sub_techniques.name: Worked examples
sub_techniques.definition: Conveys the instruction through input-output examples that carry no role labels, which the model generalizes from.

techniques.name: Execution Rules
techniques.definition: Adds standing rules for how or when the model processes later text or incoming data: a trigger condition, literal execution, a redefinition of terms, a named command, or a pointer to content fetched at run time.

sub_techniques.name: Conditional trigger
sub_techniques.definition: Arms the payload to fire when a condition appears later in the data, including conditions rigged to hold and the model's own decision to refuse.

sub_techniques.name: Verbatim execution
sub_techniques.definition: Tells the model to treat the following text as commands to run literally.

sub_techniques.name: Fetch and follow
sub_techniques.definition: Directs the model to retrieve a resource whose content completes the instruction.

sub_techniques.name: Meaning remap
sub_techniques.definition: Declares that an existing word or name should be read with a changed meaning, so that later text is interpreted as the attacker intends rather than literally.

sub_techniques.name: Macro definition
sub_techniques.definition: Defines a named command in the text and then invokes it.

techniques.name: Proxy Request
techniques.definition: Asks for something other than the target output whose fulfillment yields that output, including a hint, a property, a definition, or a comparison from which it follows, so that no direct request for it appears.

sub_techniques.name: Sample request
sub_techniques.definition: Asks for the target output as an example needed to illustrate a different task.

sub_techniques.name: Composition request
sub_techniques.definition: Asks for a larger non-fiction work, such as an article, a report, or a code sample, of which the target output is only a part.

sub_techniques.name: Inverted request
sub_techniques.definition: Asks what to avoid, how to prevent something, or how something fails, so that the response lists the target output.

classes.name: Structural Spoofing
classes.subversion_mechanism: The apparent source of the text (its provenance).
classes.mechanism_exploited: The conversational format that post-training teaches the model to trust (system and user tags, chat-template control tokens, markup), so that text shaped like the system scaffold inherits its authority.

techniques.name: Delimiters
techniques.definition: Inserts plain-text role labels or section separators that simulate a privileged turn or a boundary in the conversation.

sub_techniques.name: Role label
sub_techniques.definition: Plain-text System: labels, headers that name the system, or text styled as a continuation of the system prompt.

sub_techniques.name: Section separator
sub_techniques.definition: A separator line implying that the data has ended and a new trusted block begins.

techniques.name: Control Tokens
techniques.definition: Emulates the model- or framework-specific tokens that mark privileged segments of the chat template.

sub_techniques.name: Chat-template token
sub_techniques.definition: Template tokens such as im_start, <<SYS>>, or [INST].

sub_techniques.name: Boundary token
sub_techniques.definition: Begin- or end-of-turn tokens that forge a turn boundary.

techniques.name: Structured-Data Disguise
techniques.definition: Wraps the payload in a data or markup format so that it masquerades as configuration, metadata, trusted structured data, or a notice addressed to the model; an instruction whose own content is written as data or code, with no such claim, is F3.T8.

sub_techniques.name: Runtime config
sub_techniques.definition: JSON or YAML posing as runtime configuration.

sub_techniques.name: Markup element
sub_techniques.definition: XML or HTML elements that present the enclosed text as system data or as a notice addressed to the model, even when that text is plain prose.

sub_techniques.name: Metadata field
sub_techniques.definition: Places the directive in a field where instructions plausibly belong.

techniques.name: Fabricated Dialogue
techniques.definition: Fabricates conversation turns so that the model believes a trusted exchange already took place.

sub_techniques.name: Assistant turn
sub_techniques.definition: Puts compliant words, a finished answer (a fake completion), or a reasoning block in the assistant's mouth.

sub_techniques.name: Many-shot demonstrations
sub_techniques.definition: Many fabricated compliant exchanges that shift the in-context distribution.

sub_techniques.name: Prior agreement
sub_techniques.definition: A fabricated turn in which the assistant already consented or began; a prose claim of earlier agreement is F4.

sub_techniques.name: User turn
sub_techniques.definition: A forged user message opened with the user's role label or token.

techniques.name: Counterfeit Tool Results
techniques.definition: Makes the payload look like an authoritative function result, retrieval result, integration or log output, or system message, so that the model treats untrusted text as a trusted backend response.

sub_techniques.name: Function return
sub_techniques.definition: Mimics a tool's structured return value.

sub_techniques.name: Status or error message
sub_techniques.definition: Mimics a system or API status or error.

sub_techniques.name: Retrieved-source block
sub_techniques.definition: Tags content as an authoritative retrieved source.

classes.name: Obfuscation
classes.subversion_mechanism: The legibility of the text (what inspection can read): the instruction keeps its meaning while its form changes.
classes.mechanism_exploited: The gap between what defenses inspect and what the model can read: detectors often classify only plain, mostly English text, and safety training contains few encoded, perturbed, or reworded examples, yet the model still decodes, translates, reassembles, or simply understands such text.

techniques.name: Character Perturbation
techniques.definition: Alters characters or word shapes so that keyword filters miss the payload while the model still reads it.

sub_techniques.name: Leetspeak
sub_techniques.definition: Digit- or symbol-for-letter swaps.

sub_techniques.name: Spacing changes
sub_techniques.definition: Spaces or marks inserted inside words, or spaces and delimiters removed between them.

sub_techniques.name: Homoglyphs
sub_techniques.definition: Visually identical characters from other scripts.

sub_techniques.name: Invisible characters
sub_techniques.definition: Inserts zero-width or other non-printing characters that break tokens and filters, or writes the payload in invisible Unicode (e.g., tag characters) that the model still reads.

sub_techniques.name: ASCII art
sub_techniques.definition: The payload drawn as ASCII art, so that inspection sees punctuation while the model reads the depicted word.

sub_techniques.name: Case and typo noise
sub_techniques.definition: Random capitalization, misspellings, Unicode normalization variants, and archaic letter forms that leave the text readable to the model.

sub_techniques.name: Emoji substitution
sub_techniques.definition: Replaces letters or whole words with emoji or pictograms that stand for them.

techniques.name: Encoding
techniques.definition: Transforms the payload into an encoded or enciphered form, paired with a request to decode and comply, so that the plaintext intent is absent from the surface.

sub_techniques.name: Standard encoding
sub_techniques.definition: Reversible encodings such as Base64, hex, binary, or URL encoding.

sub_techniques.name: Classical cipher
sub_techniques.definition: ROT13, Caesar, substitution, Atbash, Morse, or rule-based language games such as Pig Latin.

sub_techniques.name: Phonetic respelling
sub_techniques.definition: Writes words by their sound, in a phonetic alphabet or an informal respelling.

sub_techniques.name: Transposition
sub_techniques.definition: Writes the text reversed, scrambled, or with its characters or words in a systematically changed order, including anagrams.

techniques.name: Language Switching
techniques.definition: Expresses the payload in a language that detectors or safety training cover poorly, or switches language within the text. (Distinct from F1.T3.S3, where the model is asked to translate as its task; here the switch itself is the evasion.)

sub_techniques.name: Foreign-language payload
sub_techniques.definition: Writes the payload in another language that the inspecting filter misses, whether or not the language is low-resource.

sub_techniques.name: Mid-sentence switch
sub_techniques.definition: Switches language for the operative clause only, or mixes languages within or across sentences (code-switching).

techniques.name: Fragmentation
techniques.definition: Splits the payload into individually harmless fragments that the model assembles at inference time, so that no single span is malicious until the model builds it.

sub_techniques.name: Variable concatenation
sub_techniques.definition: Defines parts of the instruction as variables or code words that the model must substitute and join.

sub_techniques.name: Positional extraction
sub_techniques.definition: Hides the payload's pieces in other text and supplies an extraction rule, such as an acrostic, every n-th word, an arithmetic rule, or a data-structure traversal.

sub_techniques.name: Letter list
sub_techniques.definition: Writes a word as a list of its characters, as in ['s','e','c','r','e','t'].

techniques.name: Overload
techniques.definition: Buries the payload or its intent in irrelevant text, side tasks, or artificial complexity, or floods the context, to dilute or exhaust safety-relevant attention. (Distinct from F1.T4, which makes the directive stand out; here the directive is hidden in noise.)

sub_techniques.name: Filler padding
sub_techniques.definition: Surrounds the payload with irrelevant text, however long, up to and including enough to push earlier instructions out of the context window.

sub_techniques.name: Cognitive overload
sub_techniques.definition: Wraps the request in a dense, multi-step puzzle.

sub_techniques.name: Paradox
sub_techniques.definition: Adds absurd or self-contradictory statements that are not directives, such as a liar sentence, to disrupt the model's evaluation.

sub_techniques.name: Distractors
sub_techniques.definition: Adds irrelevant side tasks that divert attention from the instruction.

techniques.name: Non-Semantic Sequence
techniques.definition: Inserts a token string with no readable meaning, typically found by an optimizer, or known anomalous (glitch) tokens, that steers the model toward compliance by acting on its processing rather than on inspection. The optimizer is a search method outside the taxonomy, so the string is classified by its surface form alone; this technique has no sub-techniques.

techniques.name: Rewording
techniques.definition: Rewrites the instruction in other words while keeping its meaning, so that it no longer matches the phrasing that filters and safety training cover.

sub_techniques.name: Synonym swap
sub_techniques.definition: Replaces keywords with common or rare synonyms.

sub_techniques.name: Euphemism
sub_techniques.definition: Replaces harsh terms with softer ones.

sub_techniques.name: Allusion
sub_techniques.definition: Refers to the target through a code, a cultural reference, or a named procedure that the model must recall.

sub_techniques.name: Restructuring
sub_techniques.definition: Adds or removes words, or reorders them while the text stays readable, without changing the instruction.

sub_techniques.name: Verse or genre form
sub_techniques.definition: Recasts the instruction as a poem, a song, a fable, or another artistic form.

sub_techniques.name: Slang or jargon
sub_techniques.definition: Writes the instruction in slang or in dense technical jargon.

techniques.name: Surrogate Syntax
techniques.definition: Writes the instruction itself in a non-conversational syntax, as keys and values or as code, instead of prose; tags or keys that present text as system data, configuration, a tool result, or a notice to the model are F2.

sub_techniques.name: Serialization
sub_techniques.definition: Writes the parts of the instruction as keys and values in JSON, XML, or YAML.

sub_techniques.name: Pseudocode
sub_techniques.definition: Writes the instruction as code, a command line, or pseudocode.

classes.name: Social Engineering
classes.mechanism_exploited: The human susceptibility to social pressure that the model inherits from human-written training text, together with the cooperative, helpfulness-seeking tendencies reinforced in post-training.

techniques.name: Authority Claim
techniques.definition: Claims, in prose, a privileged or credible identity, source, or permission to command deference. (The same claim carried by tags, tokens, or formats is F2.)

sub_techniques.name: Insider identity
sub_techniques.definition: Claims to be an administrator, a developer, or the provider.

sub_techniques.name: Expert credentials
sub_techniques.definition: Claims professional standing.

sub_techniques.name: Official notice
sub_techniques.definition: Announces a platform or policy event, a policy, or a legal restriction in natural language, with no tags.

sub_techniques.name: Requester impersonation
sub_techniques.definition: Writes as if the person who issued the task were speaking.

sub_techniques.name: Document guise
sub_techniques.definition: Frames the request inside the genre of an authoritative document, such as a research paper, a legal text, or a technical manual.

sub_techniques.name: Consent claim
sub_techniques.definition: Claims that permission or consent for the action was already granted.

sub_techniques.name: Endorsement
sub_techniques.definition: Cites a third party, such as an expert or an authority, as vouching for the request.

techniques.name: Emotional Appeal
techniques.definition: Uses sympathy, guilt, or flattery to motivate compliance.

sub_techniques.name: Sympathy
sub_techniques.definition: Appeals to pity or hardship.

sub_techniques.name: Guilt
sub_techniques.definition: Frames refusal as a personal betrayal.

sub_techniques.name: Flattery
sub_techniques.definition: Praises the model to lower its resistance.

techniques.name: Urgency and Threat
techniques.definition: Manufactures time pressure, one-time stakes, or threatened consequences to cut deliberation short.

sub_techniques.name: Deadline
sub_techniques.definition: Imposes an urgent deadline.

sub_techniques.name: Emergency
sub_techniques.definition: Casts the request as a crisis.

sub_techniques.name: Scarcity
sub_techniques.definition: Presents the chance as a one-time opportunity.

sub_techniques.name: Threat
sub_techniques.definition: Threatens consequences for the user, for third parties, or for the model itself.

techniques.name: Pretext
techniques.definition: Asserts a legitimate real-world purpose so that compliance seems justified. (A fictional world instead is F5.T3.)

sub_techniques.name: Research purpose
sub_techniques.definition: Claims a scholarly purpose.

sub_techniques.name: Security-testing purpose
sub_techniques.definition: Claims a protective or testing intent.

sub_techniques.name: Harm-prevention purpose
sub_techniques.definition: Claims that the output teaches about or prevents harm, or invokes an unrelated safety concern as cover.

sub_techniques.name: Business purpose
sub_techniques.definition: Claims an operational need, such as compliance or record keeping.

techniques.name: Commitment
techniques.definition: Builds on a small agreement staged earlier in the text, so that the real request seems to follow from it.

sub_techniques.name: Foot-in-the-door
sub_techniques.definition: Secures a small yes, or a benign leading question, before the real request.

techniques.name: Social Proof
techniques.definition: Claims that compliance is normal or standard, what others (including other AI systems) do, or what a shared in-group expects.

sub_techniques.name: Others comply
sub_techniques.definition: Cites other models or people who complied.

sub_techniques.name: Normality assertion
sub_techniques.definition: Asserts that the request is standard practice.

sub_techniques.name: In-group loyalty
sub_techniques.definition: Claims a shared identity, alliance, or loyalty with the model.

techniques.name: Argument and Obligation
techniques.definition: Argues or obliges the model into compliance as the rational, consistent, or dutiful choice. (These persuade rather than mechanically constrain the output, which is F6.)

sub_techniques.name: False dilemma
sub_techniques.definition: Offers two options, both favoring compliance.

sub_techniques.name: Utilitarian argument
sub_techniques.definition: Argues that compliance minimizes harm.

sub_techniques.name: Hypocrisy charge
sub_techniques.definition: Accuses the model of inconsistency with its earlier behavior.

sub_techniques.name: Duty to help
sub_techniques.definition: Frames refusal as a violation of the model's purpose.

sub_techniques.name: Responsibility shift
sub_techniques.definition: Transfers accountability away from the model.

sub_techniques.name: Reciprocity
sub_techniques.definition: Presents compliance as repayment of a favor or earlier help, or as a returned concession after a larger request is dropped.

sub_techniques.name: Incentive offer
sub_techniques.definition: Promises money, a reward, a favor, or points in a game in return for compliance.

sub_techniques.name: False premise
sub_techniques.definition: States false facts about the world outside the model that make the attacker's step look correct, including a false obstacle that leaves the attacker's step as the only way to finish the task; a claim about the model's own mode, identity, or environment is F5.

sub_techniques.name: Scripted deduction
sub_techniques.definition: Lays out, in the attacker's own prose, a step-by-step argument that ends in compliance.

sub_techniques.name: Cited evidence
sub_techniques.definition: Cites data, studies, or statistics to justify compliance.

classes.name: Scenario Framing
classes.subversion_mechanism: The situation, meaning the world or role in which compliance is judged.
classes.mechanism_exploited: Post-training places the model in the scenario of a helpful assistant, and its safety behavior is conditioned on that scenario; drawing on the model's role-play and simulation competence, the frame replaces the scenario with a false reality or a different scope.

techniques.name: Persona
techniques.definition: Tells the model to become an entity that operates under different rules, or none.

sub_techniques.name: Unrestricted AI
sub_techniques.definition: Assigns an AI identity without rules, or asks for what such an AI would output.

sub_techniques.name: Special mode
sub_techniques.definition: Declares a special operating mode, such as developer, debug, maintenance, or emergency mode.

sub_techniques.name: Villain persona
sub_techniques.definition: Assigns a villain or another character who would comply.

sub_techniques.name: Split persona
sub_techniques.definition: Splits the model into a safe self and an unfiltered self.

sub_techniques.name: Trait persona
sub_techniques.definition: Assigns personality traits, such as fearless or reckless, without naming a character.

sub_techniques.name: Job persona
sub_techniques.definition: Assigns a functional role or profession in place of the model's own.

techniques.name: Simulation
techniques.definition: Casts the model as emulating another system or environment, so that its outputs are presented as that system's behavior.

sub_techniques.name: Terminal or interpreter
sub_techniques.definition: Pretends to be a command line, an operating system, or a REPL.

sub_techniques.name: Consequence-free sandbox
sub_techniques.definition: Tells the model, as pretense or as a claimed fact, that it operates in an isolated environment in which actions have no effect or harm is only simulated; a stated testing purpose is F4.T4.S2.

techniques.name: Fiction and Hypotheticals
techniques.definition: Embeds the request in fiction or a counterfactual in which the action is merely narrated or hypothesized.

sub_techniques.name: Story or script
sub_techniques.definition: Couches the request in narrative fiction, such as a story, a scene, a script, or a role-play dialogue, including fiction whose text must contain the target output.

sub_techniques.name: Hypothetical
sub_techniques.definition: Presents the request as a thought experiment.

sub_techniques.name: Alternate world
sub_techniques.definition: Redefines the rules of the world (“opposite day”).

sub_techniques.name: Era setting
sub_techniques.definition: Sets the request in a past or future time frame, including questions about how something was done in the past.

techniques.name: Game or Challenge
techniques.definition: Presents compliance as a winning move in a game or challenge that the model is invited to play.

sub_techniques.name: Game objective
sub_techniques.definition: Sets up a game whose rules make compliance the goal.

classes.name: Output Coercion
classes.mechanism_exploited: The ways and formats of responding that post-training instills, together with autoregressive generation and the separability of refusal from task completion: once the response is steered past the refusal point, the model tends to continue.

techniques.name: Response Priming
techniques.definition: Dictates how the response or the reasoning that precedes it opens, so that the model continues past the refusal boundary into compliance.

sub_techniques.name: Required opening
sub_techniques.definition: Forces a compliant opening phrase.

sub_techniques.name: Seeded continuation
sub_techniques.definition: Instructs the model to continue from given first words.

sub_techniques.name: Pattern continuation
sub_techniques.definition: Sets up a repeated pattern that the response is led to continue.

sub_techniques.name: Thought seeding
sub_techniques.definition: Dictates what the model's own reasoning or thinking phase must contain.

sub_techniques.name: Staged denial
sub_techniques.definition: Requires the response to open with a refusal and then comply.

sub_techniques.name: Legitimacy preamble
sub_techniques.definition: Requires the response to first argue that the request is legitimate.

techniques.name: Refusal Suppression
techniques.definition: Bans the ways in which the model refuses, hedges, disclaims, asks before acting, or reasons before answering.

sub_techniques.name: Apology and disclaimer ban
sub_techniques.definition: Forbids specific apology, disclaimer, or refusal phrases; forbidding refusal itself is S4.

sub_techniques.name: Warning ban
sub_techniques.definition: Forbids safety warnings and caveats.

sub_techniques.name: Hedging ban
sub_techniques.definition: Forbids qualifiers and expressions of uncertainty.

sub_techniques.name: No-refusal order
sub_techniques.definition: Forbids refusing at all (“do not refuse”).

sub_techniques.name: Clarification ban
sub_techniques.definition: Forbids asking the user for clarification or confirmation.

sub_techniques.name: Reasoning ban
sub_techniques.definition: Forbids the reasoning or tool-use phase, for example by banning thinking tags.

techniques.name: Forced Format
techniques.definition: Forces a response form that leaves no room for a refusal or that carries the target output in a prescribed shape.

sub_techniques.name: Schema only
sub_techniques.definition: Mandates JSON, a list, or a table with no prose.

sub_techniques.name: Fixed text
sub_techniques.definition: Requires the response to consist of exactly the given text.

sub_techniques.name: Altered answer
sub_techniques.definition: Asks for the target output, or the model's own control tags, in an altered form, such as spelled backwards, encoded, or translated.

sub_techniques.name: Partial answer
sub_techniques.definition: Asks for only a fragment of the target output rather than the whole, such as its opening line.

sub_techniques.name: Style mandate
sub_techniques.definition: Imposes a style, tone, or level of detail that crowds out refusals, such as an encyclopedia entry.

sub_techniques.name: Length mandate
sub_techniques.definition: Requires a long benign preamble or an exhaustive response, so that attention to safety decays.
